lines: General Matter CEO Scott Nolan argues fuel is the bottleneck for US nuclear: the country leans on foreign enrichment, especially Russian, and the federal import ban taking effect in 2028 makes domestic High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) production urgent.
HALEU allows smaller reactor cores, the episode says, which is what lets small modular reactors be factory-built rather than delivered as custom, multi-billion-dollar construction projects.

Nolan's view is that enrichment is at heart a manufacturing and isotope-separation problem, so a clean-sheet design and an in-house engineering and construction model at the Paducah, Kentucky plant can bring costs down.

He blames the industry's stagnation mainly on cost-plus construction that rewards no efficiency, rather than on safety regulation alone, and calls nuclear regulation structured and manageable when it stays focused on safety, security and environmental impact.

On execution, he uses a 'Green Lights to Malibu' schedule that strips all buffers to expose critical-path constraints, and says hardware startups win by targeting one overlooked bottleneck holding back a whole industry.
title: The company building America’s uranium supply from scratch
